alternatives.transcript: One Rish session. In a moment, four Codex agents will go to work inside it. Three lanes. Planning on the left, the builders in the middle, the shared board on the right. The road map agent goes first, and its very first act is to tell the board what this demo is. Then the other three check-in, standing by, no work yet, every one of them will report to this board from here to the end. The road map writes the goal down, a to do manager that runs entirely in the browser. No back end, no build step, no dependencies. It waits until all three have checked in before handing over. A message sent to an agent that has not booted yet is simply lost. Handed to the fleet manager. That is the last order the road map gives. The build is not its job. The manager splits the work by layer. Worker one takes the page and the styling. Worker two takes all the behavior. But first, it writes a contract. Every shared ID, the markup of one to do item, and which file owns what. Two agents are about to build one page in parallel, and this is the only thing holding them together. Contract posted. The work orders go out, one to each worker, and the build starts. Watch the middle lane. Both workers are running at once, and neither has read the other's file. The board is the only thing they share. No shared memory, no lock file, no messages between them, just posts. Worker two's logic lands first, then worker one's page and stylesheet. Both sign off on the board. Neither reported back by message. The manager has been watching the board because a post cannot be missed and a message can. The manager now checks the real thing rather than the reports. Does every ID the script looks up actually exist in the markup? Now the interesting part. Verifying the manager finds a real defect. The remaining count is written twice on the page. It does not fix it itself. It names the mismatch, sends the file back to worker two, and posts that it is blocked. Worker two corrects it and signs off again. The manager rechecks, and this time, everything lines up. Every shared ID matches. Both files load. The syntax is clean. The manager signs off. The road map checks the finished app against its own acceptance list. Every action, the live count, and persistence across a reload. Four agents, one board, a working app, and all four have signed off.

paragraphs.transcript:
One Rish session. In a moment, four Codex agents will go to work inside it. Three lanes. Planning on the left, the builders in the middle, the shared board on the right. The road map agent goes first, and its very first act is to tell the board what this demo is.

Then the other three check-in, standing by, no work yet, every one of them will report to this board from here to the end. The road map writes the goal down, a to do manager that runs entirely in the browser. No back end, no build step, no dependencies. It waits until all three have checked in before handing over. A message sent to an agent that has not booted yet is simply lost.

Handed to the fleet manager. That is the last order the road map gives. The build is not its job. The manager splits the work by layer. Worker one takes the page and the styling.

Worker two takes all the behavior. But first, it writes a contract. Every shared ID, the markup of one to do item, and which file owns what. Two agents are about to build one page in parallel, and this is the only thing holding them together. Contract posted.

The work orders go out, one to each worker, and the build starts. Watch the middle lane. Both workers are running at once, and neither has read the other's file. The board is the only thing they share. No shared memory, no lock file, no messages between them, just posts.

Worker two's logic lands first, then worker one's page and stylesheet. Both sign off on the board. Neither reported back by message. The manager has been watching the board because a post cannot be missed and a message can. The manager now checks the real thing rather than the reports.

Does every ID the script looks up actually exist in the markup? Now the interesting part. Verifying the manager finds a real defect. The remaining count is written twice on the page. It does not fix it itself.

It names the mismatch, sends the file back to worker two, and posts that it is blocked. Worker two corrects it and signs off again. The manager rechecks, and this time, everything lines up. Every shared ID matches. Both files load.

The syntax is clean. The manager signs off. The road map checks the finished app against its own acceptance list. Every action, the live count, and persistence across a reload. Four agents, one board, a working app, and all four have signed off.
